newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Robotics begins shipping fast modems.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Robotics begins shipping fast modems.

text.p: U.S. Robotics Corp. said Monday it had begun shipping its long-awaited x2 modems, which provide a high-speed connection to the Internet, pushing its stock higher.

The new modems, and software that allows owners of some existing U.S. Robotics modems to upgrade their devices, enable connections of 56 kilobits per second, or about twice as fast over phone lines as today's typical 28.8-kilobit-per-second modems.
The faster modems would allow computers users to download data and pages from the Internet about twice as fast as the current 28.8 kilobit modems.
Skokie, Ill.-based U.S. Robotics is the world's largest supplier of consumer modems. U.S. Robotics stock rose $2.50 to $59.125 in afternoon trading on the Nasdaq market.

The company said it had begun shipments to North American retailers. It said it planned to demonstrate a European version of the x2 at the CeBIT trade show in Germany in March, with distribution in Europe and the Pacific Rim to follow.

Industry analysts said the release was about a week later than anticipated, but they predicted the new modems would give U.S. Robotics' stock a boost in the near term and increase revenues in its fiscal third quarter.

"The stock has been going down for the last week because you had the bears ... saying it doesn't exist or it doesn't work," said Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette analyst Eric Buck. "Now the product is out the door and dispels the stories."
"It's well ahead of competitive products," said Amar Senan, an analyst for Volpe, Welty & Co. "Certainly, for third quarter we're going to see some good numbers."
Another modem maker, Cardinal Technologies Inc., said it will ship its own modems using the x2 technology in March.
In addition, America Online Inc., the world's No. 1 online service, said it would hold field trials of the x2 technology.
"Our view has been the ISPs (Internet service providers) are the key to the uptake" of this new technology, said Rakesh Sood, an analyst for Hambrecht & Quist.
The x2 technology, however, faces a battle for acceptance against similar technology backed by an alliance of rivals led by Pittsburgh-based Rockwell International Corp.
Rockwell allies include Lucent Technologies Inc. and Motorola Inc. The alliance has announced plans to introduce 56-kilobit modems in early March.

While in the long run the modem makers are expected to agree on a common standard for 56-kilobit technology, U.S. Robotics modems are currently incompatible with modems made by those in the Rockwell alliance.

U.S. Robotics said its technology gave it a significant head start over its rivals because older modems it has been shipping since August can be converted to run the higher-speed x2 technology through a simple software upgrade.
